task 03: task 03: Configuring blink through its settings YAML (`BROKER_PORTS: [19092]`, `REST_PORT: 30104` as YAML keys). No effect and no error — the broker came up on its defaults. The same names as environment variables work immediately.

task 03: task 03: `api.version.request=false` + `broker.version.fallback=0.10.0` on a librdkafka Consumer as a way to get consumer groups working against blink. No assignment, no messages, same as the default configuration.

task 03: task 03: A pytest fixture written as `yield from _serve(...)` followed by `yield value` — that yields twice and pytest rejects it. `_serve` is a `@contextmanager` and the fixture is `with _serve(...): yield value`.

task 03: task 03: Faking a pytest item in a test with `type('m', (), {'__name__': module})` to stand in for `item.module`. `type()` overwrites `__name__` with the class name, so the stand-in never matches. `SimpleNamespace(**{'__name__': module})` works.

task 04: task 04: Bootstrapping the ledger table from a `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` string inside the runner was considered and rejected before it was written: it gives the engine's schema two homes, one of them a Python string no migration describes, and concept/06-technology.md makes the SQL project source. The one thing it would have bought — being able to record a failure of the very first migration — is worth less than the split, and the error message says outright when a failure could not be recorded.

task 04: task 04: Splitting a migration file into statements in Python was considered and rejected: a naive split on ';' breaks on semicolons inside string literals and dollar-quoted bodies, and it turned out to be unnecessary — RisingWave executes a multi-statement string sent through psycopg in one execute().

task 05: task 05: Making the SQL copy of the aggregation version the single place a downstream view reads it from. All three formulations were tried against the engine and all three are rejected on RisingWave 3.0.3 with 'Not supported: streaming nested-loop join': CROSS JOIN against the constant view, JOIN ... ON true, and a scalar subquery in the select list. Do not retry this when writing the D2 aggregation views — carry the literal and test the produced rows.

task 05: task 05: Holding the aggregation version in a one-row TABLE was considered and rejected before it was written. An UPDATE to it would rewrite the version under rows that already recorded one, and in a streaming join it would recompute downstream rows — which is exactly the forbidden 'migrate old rows forward'. A view has no writer, and changing it needs a new migration that drops and recreates it.

task 05: task 05: Giving `VersionSet` a `current()` constructor that fills the aggregation version from the constant was considered and rejected: writing a row records what produced it and replay must take what is stored, and a set completed from current constants would be indistinguishable from one that was really recorded.

task 06: task 06: Asserting in the append-changes-identity test that the first record reads back identically through BOTH the old and the new capture description. `read_capture` re-hashes the file and refuses a description that no longer matches, so the stale one raises `CaptureError` — which is the better demonstration and is what the test now asserts. Worth knowing before writing anything that holds a `Capture` across a write to its file: the description is checked on every read, deliberately.

task 06: task 06: `Capture.label` and a `CAPTURE_HASH_ALGORITHM` constant were written and then removed before reporting. Both had exactly one caller — a test — which makes them structure ahead of the increment. The algorithm is named by the field (`sha256`); the regex for a capture filename is built from `CAPTURE_SUFFIX` with `re.escape` so the suffix exists once.

task 07: task 07: Deriving the event id from the capture reference and the record offset alone, as the PRD step describes, was written and then widened before reporting — see invariant_conflicts. It is deterministic and it replays correctly, and it is still wrong: it makes two tenants' ids collide in the one store, where an INSERT onto an existing key silently upserts. Do not narrow it back.

task 07: task 07: Putting `EVENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` into the event-id digest was considered and rejected before it was written. It versions the shape of the event, not which record it is, so mixing it in would change every id the first time the shape changed and the replay guarantee would hold only until the next version bump.

task 07: task 07: Adding an `ingested_at` field to the event was considered and rejected for the same family of reasons — it would make 'a capture replayed twice produces identical rows' (task 11's test) impossible to state, and the fix would then be to exclude the field from the comparison, which is the same thing as not having it.

task 08: task 08: Putting the raw-record reference (capture digest plus offset) on `ParseFailure` was considered and rejected before it was written. It would make the adapter — which has no capture — either take a reference it does not use or hand back a narrower object the normalizer widens, i.e. two types for one thing. `normalize_capture` yields exactly one result per record in file order, so `enumerate` already gives a failure its offset, and an event carries its own.

task 08: task 08: Rendering `ParseFailure.detail` from `str(ValidationError)` was considered and rejected: Pydantic echoes the rejected input into the message, so the detail would carry a second uncontrolled copy of input the module has just refused to trust, and a fully-invalid record would produce an unbounded string with no visible truncation point. The detail is `loc: msg [type]` per error, and the raw record is kept exactly as read by whatever quarantines it. A test asserts a distinctive bad value does not appear in the detail while the field name does.

task 08: task 08: Making `flow-envelope` a pure passthrough wrapper (`{"flow": {…}}`) was considered and rejected as too weak: an adapter that does nothing but unwrap demonstrates registration but not that an adapter can map a differently-shaped record onto the same contract. It renames three scalars and re-nests the layers instead — still trivial, and it fails the cross-format equality test if the mapping is wrong (mutation-checked).

task 08: task 08: Merging the envelope's `layers` over the mapped scalars without a collision check was rejected: a `layers` key named `id` would silently replace the record's own id (or be silently dropped, depending on merge order), which is exactly the coercion the contract refuses everywhere else. A key collision is `not_this_format`, and removing that guard fails a test.

task 09: task 09: Storing the payload in a VARCHAR column was rejected before it was written. Task 08 measured that invalid UTF-8 in a line raises UnicodeDecodeError from json.loads and is reported as malformed_json — so exactly the records most worth quarantining are the ones a text column would have to refuse or decode lossily, and a quarantine row that lost the bytes that caused it cannot be diagnosed. BYTEA was probed against the engine first.

task 09: task 09: Putting a `quarantined_at TIMESTAMPTZ` on the row was considered and rejected. It would break the property task 11 is about to test (a capture replayed twice produces identical rows) for this table, and under the composite-key upsert the stored value would silently mean 'the last time this was refused' rather than 'when it was first seen' — a field that looks like provenance and is not. Arrival time is a property of an ingest run.

task 09: task 09: Writing the event id onto a quarantine row was considered and rejected. The digest computes perfectly well from tenant, sensor, capture and offset even for a refused record, which is exactly why it is tempting — and it would assert an event identity for something that never became an event, contradicting `Normalizer.normalize`'s rule that no identity is stamped on a record that never became an observation. The primary key addresses the row instead, and a test pins the field set of `QuarantinedRecord`.

task 09: task 09: Giving `ingest_capture` its own loop over `read_capture` was rejected: it would have made two places that read a capture and stamp identity, which is the parallel path `concept/03-architecture.md` forbids. Both `normalize_capture` and `ingest_capture` now go through one private `_results(capture)` generator yielding (offset, raw line, result) — the raw line has to be carried alongside because a `ParseFailure` deliberately holds no copy of the input it refused and an event holds only the parsed observation.

task 09: task 09: Letting `Quarantine.counts` compute the rate over zero records as 0.0 was rejected — it reads as 'nothing was refused' when the truth is 'nothing was read'. It raises instead, and a test pins it. `describe_capture` really can return record_count 0 (an empty file), so this is reachable.

task 10: task 10: Distinguishing 'the topic already exists' by catching KafkaException and comparing to KafkaError.TOPIC_ALREADY_EXISTS. It was written and it fails against blink 0.2.0 — see lessons. Do not retry it; ask Metadata first.

task 10: task 10: Asserting 'a second drain of a drained topic returns nothing' immediately after the first drain. It passes about half the time. The first version of tests/test_broker.py did exactly this and failed on its second run; the deadline-and-control version replaced it.

task 10: task 10: A mutation that appended a trailing space to the payload on the wire path did NOT fail any test, and that is correct rather than a hole: the store keeps the PARSED observation, and trailing whitespace is not part of a record. Worth knowing before someone adds a byte-level wire assertion that would only pin JSON serialization trivia.

task 10: task 10: Adding HELENA_OUTPUT_TOPIC 'while the config file is open' was considered and rejected before it was written — a key nothing reads has one value and no way to be wrong, and the egress invariant is enforced by the boundary test instead.

task 10: task 10: Giving `helena.broker` any knowledge of the ingest message shape was rejected. It carries bytes and header bytes; `IngestMessage` in helena.normalizer is the only thing that knows the headers mean a raw-record reference. That split is what makes the broker module swappable rather than merely wrapped, and it also avoids the import cycle a shared RawRecordReference would have created.

task 10: task 10: Making `ingest_messages` capture-scoped (taking a Capture, as the PRD's step-4 wording suggests) was rejected. A consumer has no capture file, and requiring one would have made live ingestion impossible by construction. The reconciliation against the capture happens after the run, in `ingest_counts`, which is the only place a file is needed.
lessonsLearned: task 00: The two earlier task-00 sessions failed at 0 s with exit 1 and wrote nothing to disk. The cause is in prds/logs/*.stderr: '--dangerously-skip-permissions cannot be used with root/sudo privileges for security reasons'. It was a runner invocation problem, not a code problem — nothing had been half-built.

task 00: bin/blink starts from a settings YAML containing just `{}`. Defaults observed: broker ports 9094 and 9092 (metadata advertises 9094), REST port 30004, retention 5m, 1 partition per topic, kafka_hostname 'localhost'. It prints a large ANSI banner to stdout — pipe it to a file, not into a terminal you are reading.

task 00: confluent-kafka against blink 0.2.0: produce to a non-existent topic silently stays queued through flush(10). Create the topic with AdminClient first. Consumption works with assign(TopicPartition(topic, 0, OFFSET_BEGINNING)); subscribe() returned nothing.
task 00: psycopg 3 needs autocommit=True for RisingWave DDL to be usable in the same session, and `FLUSH` after an INSERT before the row is readable from a table.

task 00: requires-python is pinned '>=3.12,<3.13', not '>=3.12'. RisingWave links libpython3.12.so.1.0 and the ABI does not survive a minor bump; the upper bound turns that into a resolution error instead of a silent runtime failure.
task 00: The maturity-label test reads the docstring with ast, not by importing the module, so a module with a broken import fails the import test rather than confusing the label test.

task 00: pytest is configured with filterwarnings = ["error"] — a new dependency that emits a DeprecationWarning on import will break the suite. That is deliberate (fail loud), but worth knowing before blaming the test.

task 01: task 01: `from pydantic_core import core_schema` FAILS tests/test_dependency_boundary.py — pydantic-core is a separate distribution and only 'pydantic' is in APPROVED_RUNTIME_DISTRIBUTIONS. Build custom Pydantic behaviour from the `pydantic` namespace instead: Annotated[T, PlainSerializer(...)] plus ConfigDict(arbitrary_types_allowed=True) covers a wrapper type without __get_pydantic_core_schema__.

task 01: task 01: Pydantic echoes the rejected input in a ValidationError ('input_value=...'), so a credential passed to the wrong field leaks into a traceback. Verified by running it. Every settings model sets ConfigDict(hide_input_in_errors=True); any later model that holds a Secret must do the same.

task 01: task 01: The live model endpoint offers 33 models and both LLM_MODEL_TRIAGE and LLM_MODEL_ANALYST are among them; the two agents currently share one LLM_URL and one LLM_TOKEN and differ only by model. GET {LLM_URL}/models with a Bearer token is a cheap way to check a model id exists before spending a completion on finding out.

task 01: task 01: ThreatFox API v1 (https://threatfox-api.abuse.ch/api/v1/) requires the key as an `Auth-Key` HEADER — the same request without it returns HTTP 401. But {"query": "get_ioc", "id": "41"} came back 200 with query_status 'unknown_operation', so that operation name is wrong for the current API. The feed-loader task must fetch the current query vocabulary rather than assume one; only the auth mechanism is confirmed here.
task 01: task 01: The local .env now also carries HELENA_TENANT and HELENA_SENSOR (added by this task). Anything that needs tenant or sensor reads settings.identity, never os.environ.

task 01: task 01: Settings.load(environ=..., env_file=...) takes both by keyword so tests are hermetic; passing env_file=None skips the file entirely. A test that resolves settings without passing environ would read the machine's real environment — do not write one.

task 02: task 02: `urllib.error.HTTPError` carries the full request URL on `.url` and `.filename` but NOT in `str(exception)`. So logging an exception's message is safe and logging its attributes or its repr is not — which is the opposite of the intuition that the message is the risky part. Verified against a real 404.

task 02: task 02: An `HTTPError` IS the response object and holds the connection open. Returning one from a helper without calling `.close()` leaves an unclosed socket, and because pytest is configured with `filterwarnings = ["error"]` the resulting ResourceWarning surfaces as an unraisable-exception failure in whatever test happens to run later — in this session, an unrelated AST test. If a test fails with PytestUnraisableExceptionWarning about a socket, look for an unclosed urllib response, not at the test that failed.

task 02: task 02: `urllib.parse.urlencode` percent-encodes `*`, so a redaction marker rebuilt through it comes out as `%2A%2A%2Aredacted%2A%2A%2A`. Pass `safe="*"` to keep `***redacted***` readable in a log line.

task 02: task 02: Redacting a URL structurally must NOT guess at path segments. This project fetches URLs whose path segments are sha256 hashes (mb-api.abuse.ch/downloads/<sha256>/), and an entropy or length heuristic would redact exactly the provenance the fetch exists to record. Redaction of a path segment is by registered value only; the stated consequence is that an unregistered credential in a path is not redacted, and the answer to that is that credentials only enter through helena.config.

task 02: task 02: A test that asserts a real credential is absent must not put the credential in the assertion expression — pytest's assertion rewriting prints both operands on failure, so `assert key not in output` leaks the key at the exact moment the redaction failed. Compute the boolean first: `leaked = key in output; assert not leaked, "..."`.

task 02: task 02: The current ThreatFox bulk export at https://threatfox.abuse.ch/export/json/recent/ serves 200 with no credential at all. Combined with task 01's finding that the API v1 wants an `Auth-Key` HEADER, there is currently no confirmed abuse.ch endpoint that takes the key in the URL path. Do not build the loader around one without fetching first.

task 03: task 03: The libpython ABI mismatch has NO runtime symptom. With libpython3.14 symlinked onto libpython3.12.so.1.0, `./bin/risingwave --version` prints the correct string and exits 0, `single_node --in-memory` starts, binds the PostgreSQL port and answers `SELECT version()` with the identical string, and nothing appears in its log. A MISSING library is loud ('error while loading shared libraries'); a WRONG one is silent. Only a structural check discriminates: `ldd bin/risingwave`, then sha256 the file the SONAME resolved to. `uv run scripts/dev_check.py --binaries-only` does exactly that.

task 03: task 03: RisingWave `single_node --in-memory` is usable in well under a second, not tens of seconds: connection accepted at 0.50 s, `SELECT version()` at 0.51 s, three RUNNING workers in rw_catalog.rw_worker_nodes at 0.53 s, and a full CREATE TABLE / INSERT / FLUSH / SELECT / DROP round trip at 0.65 s. Earlier sessions (this one included, at first) slept 30-40 s after starting it on an assumption nobody had measured.

task 03: task 03: `--listen-addr` moves only the PostgreSQL port. Meta and compute bind fixed 5690 and 5688, so a second RisingWave cannot run alongside the first whatever port you give it — it panics with 'failed to bind `grpc-meta-leader-service` to 127.0.0.1:5690: Address already in use'. That is why tests/conftest.py uses an already-answering instance instead of always starting a throwaway one.

task 03: task 03: The mysterious `secrets/` directory at the project root that task 0 noticed is RisingWave's. The frontend's `temp_secret_file_dir` defaults to `./secrets`, relative to the engine's working directory. dev-up runs it in `.run/engine/` and the fixtures run it in a pytest tmp dir, so it does not appear at the root any more.

task 03: task 03: RisingWave 3.0.3 phones home to telemetry.risingwave.dev by default. `scripts/risingwave.toml` with `[server] telemetry_enabled = false` turns it off, and the resolved value is visible in the engine's config dump in the log.

task 03: task 03: Blink is configured by ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES, not by the settings YAML — `--settings <path>` is required but the settings come from the environment. The full set is BROKER_PORTS, REST_PORT, KAFKA_HOSTNAME, RETENTION, KAFKA_CFG_NUM_PARTITIONS, ENABLE_CONSUMER_GROUPS, HEAP_MEMORY_FACTOR, KAFKA_MEM_HEAP, USE_LAST_ACCESSED_OFFSET, CHECK_FOR_SKIPPED_BATCHES, OBLITERATION_WARNING_INTERVAL_MINUTES. Unknown YAML keys are accepted silently. Blink prints the Settings struct it resolved on startup, so the log is the authority.

task 03: task 03: The reason blink's `subscribe()` returns nothing (task 00 found this and did not investigate) is exact: blink 0.2.0 CLOSES THE TCP CONNECTION on `FindCoordinatorRequest v2`. Metadata succeeds, the coordinator lookup gets a disconnect, the consumer loops in query-coord forever with no error. ENABLE_CONSUMER_GROUPS=true does not help (blink does start its consumer-group background tasks; the disconnect is unchanged), and neither does api.version.request=false with broker.version.fallback=0.10.0. The pinned commit 645c814f is literally titled 'Restrict the FindCoordinator version range to supported versions'. Consume with assign(TopicPartition(topic, partition, offset)) and manage offsets yourself.
task 03: task 03: `AdminClient.list_consumer_groups()` against blink SUCCEEDS and returns an empty result, so it is not a probe for the above. Do not use it to detect the limitation.

task 03: task 03: Neither binary can confirm its own provenance — blink does not embed its commit (it reports `blink 0.2.0`, banner `v0.2.LOCAL`) and RisingWave's v3.0.3 tag ships two Linux assets, only one of which is on disk. So the sha256 in docs/versions.md is the pin and the version strings are a sanity check. Both upstream facts were confirmed through the GitHub API rather than assumed: the tag exists (published 2026-08-17) and commit 645c814fe18edc43fc1d619d3f90f646ba18bedd exists in cleafy/blink (2025-10-06).

task 03: task 03: Embedded Python UDFs are off by default in RisingWave 3.0.3 (`[udf] enable_embedded_python_udf`), and with them on, the first SELECT that evaluates one kills the whole engine process with nothing in its log — with the pinned library as well as with a mismatched one. Do not read a UDF crash as an ABI problem, and do not build anything on Python UDFs.

task 03: task 03: pytest ordering is imposed in tests/conftest.py: unit tests, then tests/test_infrastructure.py, then any other test carrying the `integration` marker (registered in pyproject.toml because --strict-markers is on). The real guarantee that nothing addresses a dead endpoint is the fixture, which does the readiness wait before it yields.

task 04: task 04: RisingWave 3.0.3 has NO transaction around DDL, and psycopg happily sends a multi-statement string to it. Measured: `CREATE TABLE a; CREATE TABLE a` as one execute() creates `a`, then raises DuplicateObject — and `a` is still there afterwards. Any migration file with more than one statement can therefore leave the store half-migrated, which is why the ledger carries a `failed` status rather than pretending a file is atomic.

task 04: task 04: RisingWave supports CREATE SCHEMA, `SET search_path TO <s>`, `current_schema()`, `information_schema.tables` (with table_schema, and it lists views and materialized views too) and DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE. That is the way to get an isolated empty store per test on the ONE engine a machine can run — tests/conftest.py::engine_schema does it. `rw_catalog.rw_tables` also works but has no `relation_name`/`relation_type` columns; `rw_catalog.rw_relations` rejects both.

task 04: task 04: An INSERT onto an existing PRIMARY KEY in RisingWave is an UPSERT — it overwrites the row and raises nothing. Do not rely on a primary key to reject a duplicate write; if a duplicate must be refused, the code has to refuse it. And a row inserted into a RisingWave table is not readable until `FLUSH` (confirmed again here: without it the ledger reports a just-applied migration as pending).

task 04: task 04: Selecting from a table that does not exist in RisingWave raises psycopg UndefinedObject with sqlstate 42704, not the PostgreSQL 42P01 UndefinedTable. Test the catalog (`information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = current_schema()`) rather than catching an exception class or a sqlstate.

task 04: task 04: `uv run scripts/dev_check.py --wait N` waits for the engine AND the broker. Waiting on it with only the engine running blocks for the full N seconds and then still succeeds if a stray broker is up. To wait for just the engine, connect with psycopg in a loop.

task 04: task 04: The migration ledger `helena_schema_migrations` is migration 0001 itself, not a bootstrap constant in Python — so the engine's schema has one home. The consequence, and it is in the error text: if 0001 fails there is nowhere to record that it failed, and `MigrationFailed.recorded_in_ledger` is False for exactly that case.

task 05: task 05: RisingWave 3.0.3 cannot read a one-row constant view from a STREAMING query. `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW m AS SELECT t.x, v.c FROM t CROSS JOIN const_view v` fails with 'Not supported: streaming nested-loop join', and so do `JOIN const_view ON true` and `(SELECT c FROM const_view)` as a scalar subquery. A batch SELECT over the same view is fine. Consequence for D2: an aggregation view stamps the version as a literal in its own definition, and the test asserts the produced rows equal helena.versions.AGGREGATION_VERSION. tests/test_versions.py pins the limitation.

task 05: task 05: `information_schema.columns.column_default` is NULL in RisingWave 3.0.3 even for a column that really has a DEFAULT and really applies it — `CREATE TABLE d (x INT PRIMARY KEY, agg VARCHAR NOT NULL DEFAULT 'v1'); INSERT INTO d (x) VALUES (7)` stores ('7','v1'), and `SHOW CREATE TABLE d` shows the default text, but the information_schema column is empty. So a column default cannot be checked from information_schema; insert a row and read it back, or read SHOW CREATE TABLE.

task 05: task 05: A Pydantic field named `model_version` (or anything starting with `model_`) emits a UserWarning about the protected `model_` namespace, and pytest is configured with filterwarnings = ["error"], so it is a test failure. `ConfigDict(protected_namespaces=())` is the fix and nothing here shadows a BaseModel method.

task 05: task 05: `Redactor([])` raises by design — a redactor with nothing registered would silently redact nothing. A test that needs a StructuredLogger must register a value; a fake one is enough when the test is not about redaction.

task 05: task 05: Mutation-check an equality test between two copies of a constant before believing it. Flipping AGGREGATION_VERSION alone and watching the engine test fail is what distinguishes a real assertion from one that compares a value with itself.

task 05: task 05: A plain `CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT 'x' AS c` works in RisingWave, shows up in `information_schema.tables` with table_type 'VIEW', and its text is in `rw_catalog.rw_views.definition`. Selecting from it is the way to assert the constant; the catalog text is not needed and would be the 'assert on SQL text' mistake.

task 06: task 06: `model_dump(exclude_unset=True) == json.loads(line)` over every record of a real capture is the only test that actually demonstrates 'no invented fields' — a field list a human reads cannot fail, and this does, per record, naming the record. Use `exclude_unset` rather than `exclude_none`: the first is a statement about what arrived, the second about what happens to be null now.

task 06: task 06: Pydantic 2.13 `strict=True`, measured for both Python objects and `model_validate_json`: `1` into a float field is ACCEPTED (so an integer epoch second still validates), `"1.5"` into a float is rejected, `1.0` into an int is rejected, `True` into an int is rejected, and a string into a str-typed field that arrived as a number is rejected. Strict mode is therefore usable on real telemetry without loosening anything — the one widening it keeps is exactly the one you want.

task 06: task 06: `data/ingest/flow-sample.jsonl` measured field-by-field: 62 records, top-level keys id/ts/td/ip always, then udp 31, tcp 31, dns 30, tls 25, http2 15, http 11. Six layer combinations occur — dns alone 30, tls+http2 15, http alone 6, tls+http 5, tls alone 5, and ONE record (`udp.28`, SSDP to 239.255.255.250) with no application layer at all. `ip.proto` agrees with which of tcp/udp is present on all 62. Empty-but-observed arrays are real in this data: `tls.csvers` and `tls.ssvers` are empty on almost every TLS observation and `tcp.24` has `tls.alpn == []`. There are no JSON nulls anywhere in the file.

task 06: task 06: The HTTP layers differ structurally, not incidentally: `num` and `content_len` appear on HTTP/1 request and response observations and on none of the 21 HTTP/2 requests or 47 HTTP/2 responses. `content_type` and `server` are absent on some HTTP/2 responses and present on all HTTP/1 ones — the same fact over two versions, so they are optional on both. That cross-version counter-example is the only evidence in the sample about which fields are genuinely optional.

task 06: task 06: `data/ingest/README.md` is a datasheet holding the sample's sha256, byte size and record count, and it says the checksum IS the version. That makes it a second copy of a constant, so `test_the_sample_capture_matches_its_datasheet` parses those three rows out of the markdown and asserts them against `describe_capture` — the project's 'two copies asserted equal' rule applied to a fixture instead of to a version.

task 06: task 06: `tests/test_package_layout.py` uses `rglob("*.py")` and compares file STEMS, so a subpackage (`normalizer/records.py`) fails the layout test on the stem `records`. Everything a component owns goes in its one module file, or `COMPONENT_MODULES`/`SUPPORT_MODULES` has to be edited — which is the intended friction.

task 07: task 07: Pydantic 2.13 `strict=True` still ACCEPTS a plain dict for a nested model field (measured: `EventIdentity(..., raw_record={'capture_sha256': ..., 'record_offset': 0})` validates). Strict mode constrains scalar coercion, not model construction from a mapping. Worth knowing before writing a test that relies on a dict being rejected — it will pass for the wrong reason.

task 07: task 07: A tenant is an operator-supplied string, so any delimiter can occur inside one. Joining identity parts with a separator before hashing makes `tenant='a'/sensor='b:c'` and `tenant='a:b'/sensor='c'` collide into one id for two tenants. Consuming across more than one partition. The pinned broker runs one partition per topic and fanning out would be ordering machinery for a case that does not exist; the partition is a parameter with one value in use.
Any use of blink's REST port (30004). Deliberately unreachable, and tests/test_broker.py asserts helena/broker.py imports no HTTP or socket module.
10.makes_buildable: Task 11 (capture replay driver) has everything but the CLI: `IngestMessage.headers()` is the producer side of the wire contract, `BrokerProducer.create_topic/publish/flush` is the publishing path (with a flush that raises instead of silently losing a capture), and `ingest_counts(...)` is the produced-versus-materialized report its step 3 asks for. Task 12 (flatten-layer views) has `helena_normalized_events` to build over, with the observation as JSONB that preserves absent-vs-empty (measured over all 62 real records) and `->`/`?` navigation working. Task 46/47 (sink and egress) has the wrapper and, more usefully, the boundary test that already covers the egress end — a Kafka client in `sink.py` is a test failure today.
10.next_session_should_know: The ingress path is: BrokerProducer.publish(topic, message.payload, message.headers()) -> BrokerConsumer.consume(topic) -> IngestMessage.from_headers(value=..., headers=...) -> Normalizer.ingest_messages(messages, events, quarantine) -> ingest_counts(capture=..., consumed=..., events=..., quarantine=...). The whole of it is exercised end to end in tests/test_normalizer.py against the real broker and engine; copy `publish()` and `consumed_messages()` from that file into the replay driver rather than reinventing the framing. Eight things that will bite otherwise. (1) HELENA_INGEST_TOPIC is a NEW required variable — it is in helena.config.VARIABLES, .env.example and the local .env, and any test that builds an environment dict must include it or Settings.load fails naming it. (2) `settings.infrastructure.ingest_topic` is where it lands; there is no output topic and adding one is task 46's. (3) `helena.broker` is the ONLY module allowed to import confluent_kafka — tests/test_broker.py fails on a second importer, on an unapproved name bound from it, on an HTTP or socket import inside broker.py, and on ANY address-shaped string literal anywhere in src/helena (including a `:9092`-style port). Put an address in configuration, and put a measured fact about the broker in a docstring (docstrings are excluded from that scan on purpose). (4) `create_topic` asks Metadata first — do not rewrite it as create-and-catch, blink answers a duplicate create with an unparseable response. (5) `publish` is asynchronous; nothing has reached the broker until `flush()`, which RAISES on outstanding or refused messages. The `with BrokerProducer(...)` block flushes on clean exit. (6) The reclaim after a drain is asynchronous — do not write a test asserting a topic is empty immediately, and do not build a retry that re-reads a topic. Replay publishes the retained capture. (7) `Quarantine.record` changed signature: it takes `reference=RawRecordReference(...)` now, not `capture=`/`offset=`. (8) `IngestCounts` refuses a set that does not reconcile and `complete is False` means records were lost between the producer and the store — the capture is still on disk, replay it. Migration 0004 creates `helena_normalized_events` (TABLE, PK tenant/sensor/capture_sha256/record_offset, observation JSONB) and `helena_ingest_counts` (plain VIEW, read by EventStore.normalized and the reconciliation). The flatten layer of task 12 builds over the table, not the view. Docs: docs/decisions/0014-the-ingest-topic-message.md is the wire contract and the broker-is-not-a-store measurements; docs/runbook.md gained §7 (ingest and the four counters) and its §3 now carries the corrected CreateTopics and reclaim measurements; the old §7 troubleshooting table is now §8 and has four new rows.
10.summary: The ingest path now runs over the wire: `helena.broker` is a thin producer/consumer wrapper that is the only module in the package importing a Kafka client, `helena.normalizer` consumes the ingest topic and writes validated events into `helena_normalized_events` (migration 0004), and `IngestCounts` reconciles four numbers from four places — the capture file, the run, `helena_ingest_counts` and `helena_ingest_quarantine_counts`. A capture published to a real blink topic, consumed back and stored in a real RisingWave produces rows identical to the same capture read from disk.
